titles.l2: Some things are not in a line

kernelIdea: Induction needs a statement indexed by integers n ≥ n₀ and a way to connect case k+1 back to case k. Statements about all real numbers are not candidates.

kernels.l1: Dominoes have to be in a line. Some things are not in a line.
kernels.l2: Dominoes only work if they are in a row, one after another. A claim about every number one at a time can be done with dominoes. A claim about everything at once cannot.
kernels.l3: Induction needs two things: cases lined up one after another, counted by whole numbers, and a way to get from one case to the next. A claim about every number on the number line has no next case, so induction cannot touch it.
kernels.l4: Induction needs a claim made about the whole numbers one at a time, and a link carrying each case to the next. A claim about every real number has no next case, so induction has nothing to walk along.
kernels.l5: Induction needs two things: a claim made about the whole numbers one at a time, and a usable link from each case to the next. Sums, products and step-by-step definitions supply that link; a claim about every real number has no next case at all.
kernels.l6: Induction applies when the cases come with a first one and each has a next — exactly what supplies the two halves of the proof. Strong induction and induction on how a thing is built keep that requirement while widening what "next" is allowed to mean.
kernels.l7: Induction applies exactly when the statements come one per whole number and each case is reachable from the one before. Without that step-by-step structure there is nothing to walk along.
kernels.l8: Induction needs a claim indexed by the counting numbers *and* a link from each case to the next. When the link reaches further back, strong induction supplies it; when the objects are built by rules rather than counted, structural induction does.
